summary: Raymond Weitekamp presents on recursive coding agents, applying RLM principles to coding agents for higher reliability. He argues the bottleneck is not intelligence but reliable outcome delivery, citing a personal example where Claude Code delivered a working SaaS app one day but emptied his Solana wallet the next. The thesis, borrowed from Alex Zeng and Omar Khattab at MIT, frames today's agents as mismanaged geniuses — the missing layer is how to specify, manage, reuse, and verify work. RLMs are defined by treating context as the object of computation, a marriage of tool calling and reasoning via a REPL where the model explores externalized prompts symbolically and spawns sub-agents for recursive decomposition. Performance advantages are striking: RLMs process tens of millions of tokens, function as a top-10 memory system without modification, and on Long CoT, Qwen 3.59B as an RLM beat Opus and GPT-5.4. Symbolica's Agentica scored 30%+ on ARC AGI-3 versus 2-3% for frontier models. Weitekamp provides a rubric: executable environment, externalized prompt, code calling the model, model-chosen decomposition, and symbolic state. He then addresses the debate over whether Claude Code with sub-agents is already an RLM — originally no, but now arguably yes thanks to dynamic workflows released weeks ago, which enable recursive workflow patterns. He wrote two Claude Code workflows: a hardcoded map-reduce (not an RLM) and a deep-research-over-file-system pattern (an RLM). Beyond Claude Code, he introduces OpenProse, a markdown-based programming language compiled by coding agents rather than computers, with a `prose write` command that generates .prose.md files. OpenProse can turn any agent with a file system and sub-agents into an RLM, explicitly declaring sub-agent work, verifying results in parent sessions, and wiring skills and tools as explicit dependencies. Example use cases include repo-scale migrations, recursive directory analysis, audits, bug sweeps, adversarial red-team agents, and golden-session capture — deconstructing a successful session into a reusable Prose workflow for reliable replay. He concludes with three takeaways: trust requires reliability (the next step is behavioral orchestration, not raw intelligence), RLMs unify tool calling and reasoning as a new paradigm of inference-time compute, and coding agents can be RLMs but are not automatically — OpenProse and Claude Code dynamic workflows both provide paths to recursive coding agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Motivation
sections.summary: Weitekamp introduces the talk and motivates the need for reliable agent outcomes. He shares a personal anecdote where Claude Code delivered a working SaaS app one day but emptied his Solana wallet the next, illustrating that the bottleneck is not intelligence but reliable outcome delivery. He introduces the thesis that today's agents are 'mismanaged geniuses,' a framing from Alex Zeng and Omar Khattab at MIT.

sections.title: What Are Recursive Language Models?
sections.summary: Defines RLMs as systems where the context itself is the object of computation — a marriage of tool calling and reasoning. The full prompt is a variable (files), and a REPL allows symbolic exploration rather than loading everything into context. Sub-RLMs/sub-LLMs perform symbolic manipulation to decompose problems and work back up to answers. Weitekamp positions RLMs as the next paradigm of inference-time compute.

sections.title: RLM Performance & Benchmarks
sections.summary: Showcases RLM performance: processing tens of millions of tokens, functioning as a top-10 memory system without modification, and achieving state-of-the-art on Long CoT where Qwen 3.59B as an RLM beat Opus and GPT-5.4. Symbolica's Agentica scored 30%+ on ARC AGI-3 vs 2-3% for frontier models within hours, prompting controversy. RLMs are described as arguably too hot to benchmark, leading to separate open harness leaderboards.

sections.title: RLM Criteria & Rubric
sections.summary: Presents a rubric for what constitutes an RLM: executable environment, externalized prompt, code calling the model, model-chosen decomposition, and symbolic state. Plain LLMs, RAG, hardcoded map-reduces, and standard coding agent sub-agents are evaluated as close but not fully meeting RLM criteria because the model does not decide problem decomposition.

sections.title: Recursive Coding Agents & Early Experiments
sections.summary: Explores applying RLM principles to coding agents. Addresses the debate over whether Claude Code with sub-agents is already an RLM. Presents experiments: wrapping Alex's RLM package as a CLI tool, and building Y-pi — a fully recursive coding agent where pi calls pi at configurable depth, now achievable via a pure pi extension. Surveys related projects including DSPy pi.rlm and AXE.

sections.title: Unix RLM & OpenProse Overview
sections.summary: Highlights Dan at OpenProse's Unix RLM, a pure bash implementation where the environment is the Linux file system, illustrating another angle of RLM possibility. Introduces OpenProse as a language that can convert any coding agent into an RLM, with a harness in the OpenProse repo supporting Codex SDK or Claude Code for RLM-style execution of prose programs.

sections.title: Is Claude Code an RLM? Dynamic Workflows
sections.summary: Addresses the recurring question of whether Claude Code is an RLM. Originally the answer was no, but with dynamic workflows released weeks ago, Omar Khattab congratulated Anthropic that Claude Code is finally an RLM. Weitekamp recommends the blog post 'A Harness for Every Task' showing six workflow patterns. He wrote two Claude Code workflows: a hardcoded map-reduce (explicitly not an RLM) and a deep-research-over-file-system pattern (an RLM).

sections.title: OpenProse: Turning Any Agent into an RLM
sections.summary: Introduces OpenProse in depth: a programming language compiled by coding agents rather than computers, using markdown specs in logical English with no special syntax. The `prose write` command generates .prose.md files via Claude Code, Codex, pi, or any coding agent. OpenProse can turn any agent with a file system and sub-agents into an RLM, explicitly declaring sub-agent work, verifying results in parent sessions, and wiring skills and tools as explicit dependencies to ensure sub-agents are properly configured.

sections.title: Recursive Coding Agent Examples & Golden Sessions
sections.summary: Showcases practical examples: repo-scale migrations with parallel swarms, recursive directory deep research/analysis, audits, bug sweeps, and adversarial red-team agents. Introduces golden-session capture — a Prose program that deconstructs a successful agent session into a reusable Prose workflow, enabling reliable replay of high-performance outcomes over and over.

sections.title: Conclusion & Takeaways
sections.summary: Concludes with three takeaways: trust requires reliability and the next step is behavioral orchestration not raw intelligence; RLMs represent a new paradigm of inference-time compute unifying tool calling and reasoning with recursive iteration; coding agents can be RLMs but are not automatically — Claude Code dynamic workflows and OpenProse both provide paths. Closes with 'recurse responsibly.'
